en: The Scripture on the Three Storehouses Spoken by the Buddha, translated by the Western Brahmin Dharadatta,
Jñānagupta, and others, by imperial decree.
First is the kitchen of self-awakening and spontaneity through supreme compassion;
second is the kitchen of non-conceptualization for *pratyekabuddhas*, those of the four fruits, and *śrāvakas*;
third is the kitchen of spontaneity that is neither existent nor non-existent and devoid of a self.
If one can recite these three methods for the kitchen,
it will cause one to never hunger and to live in serene, eternal life.
First, one should have faith in the Triple Gem;
one should revere the Triple Gem;
and one must constantly pay homage to the Triple Gem.
Day and night, with diligent and constant mindfulness that never ceases,
one should practice filial support for teachers, monks, parents, and kinsmen,
and be able to study the six pāramitās.
Only after not sparing even one's own body or life can this method of the Three Storehouses be transmitted;
it is the natural storehouse of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the three periods of time.
This kitchen of compassion, eternally abiding, serene, and unmoving throughout kalpas,
is the Dharma of the Three Kitchens. When the Buddha was about to enter nirvana,
he proclaimed it before all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the ten directions and amidst the great assembly of the eight classes of beings.
He spoke this Dharma of the Compassion of Heaven’s Kitchen, which has been constant, serene, and unmoving throughout kalpas, for all Buddhas of the past, present, and future.
Then he spoke these verses:
The single breath harmonizes the Great Harmony; Attaining the One Way, all become Great. Harmony is the Original Unity.
The profound principle is identical to the profound limit; this is the verse of the Tree of Long Life.
Recite it ninety times.
Do not use the mind to contemplate the mind, nor seek a state of no-thought; let the mind remain without further thought.
One should maintain this matter in this way; this is the "Verse on the Unheated Fire.
Recite it thirty times:
The various fetters of food-gases and wind-gases, Not those long-settled fetters— The gases return to their original gases.
"Wherever the accumulation occurs, there one should discharge it; this is the central land of non-hunger.
(Verse) Recite one hundred and twenty times:
*Liuli zhi liuzhi* (理理志理志), *jixiu bubumai* (積修不扶埋), *zhier buzhi zhi* (志而不修志).
"Past karma has no past wisdom"—this is the "unfailing golden verse.
Recite it seventy times.
Do not take the mind as an object for the mind; do not dwell in the cessation of objects; when the mind is present, do not harbor a notion of "mind."
"Truth is to guard the profound source; this is the verse for not thirsting for water.
Recite this fifty times.
This is the kitchen of compassion.
When the Buddha was on the verge of entering *nirvāṇa*,
amidst the assembly of all Buddhas of the ten directions and the eight classes of beings,
he proclaimed this eternal, self-manifesting triple-storehouse of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the three periods— past, present, and future.
Neither hungry nor thirsty;
neither cold nor hot;
neither old nor young.
All the noble assembly is serene and unmoving, naturally possessing the three celestial kitchens.
If one can receive and uphold the name of even one celestial kitchen,
or recite it day after day, [one shall attain these benefits].
They do not think of food or drink;
some may go for a hundred days without eating,
while others may go for ten years, a hundred years, or even a thousand or ten thousand years.
They contemplate this for as many eons as there are atoms;
they abide eternally and immovably, without thoughts of food or drink,
being exactly equal and no different from the Land of Immeasurable Life of Amitābha Buddha.
The Buddha told the great assembly:
"Those who practice this Dharma need only maintain a mind of faith and reverence for the Triple Gem.
They must be able to enter deep mountains to study the Way."
Only then may this Dharma be propagated and circulated.
If there are those who harbor doubts, lack faith, or slander it,
one must not transmit it to them at will.
Fearing that those who harbor slander might fall into the evil realms,
one must not transmit this recklessly into the world.
One should recite it ninety times for the eastern direction, and so on, down to fifty times for the northern direction.
This completes one recitation.
If one has not yet reached satiety, one may recite further as above,
but no more than two times in total.
Immediately, they were satiated and free from hunger and thirst.
When reciting the verses, they always began at the hour of Tiger (寅).
Starting from the hour of Human Settlement (人定), they recited them in four sessions throughout the night.
The number of recitations is as previously described.
Furthermore, when first wishing to recite,
one should cause the mouth to move and the tongue to turn, thereby breaking the silence of silent recitation.
There will be saliva that can be swallowed down.
During the period from the first day to the third day,
the color of the urine may become reddish.
Do not consider this strange.
When he first began reciting it, by the third day his physical strength was utterly depleted.
After these three days, one will immediately attain [the power of] seven days.
Once the seven days of warming have passed, the strength of the body gradually increases;
when the rite is accomplished, it is not appropriate to recite it.
For every hundred days since then, I have dreamed of obtaining the finest flavors in the world and being fully satiated by them;
I have also smelled celestial fragrances.
Upon completing three hundred days, my spiritual power was perfected.
If one desires to eat, one eats; if not, one does not hunger.
The *Buddha-sūtra on the Three Methods of the Celestial Kitchen* (Fóshuō sānchúfǎ yījuǎn) contains a full account of the names of these celestial kitchens.
This version consists of five lines of verse.
This is the name of the Celestial Kitchen.
This dharma was received through the oral instructions of the Master Jñānagupta in the south;
it was obtained with a single word.
The third word attains fire;
the fifth word attains water;
the seventh word attains metal.
Recite "Obtained it from the Wood" nine times for the Eastern Wood;
recite it thirty times for the Southern Fire.
Recite one hundred and twenty times for Earth in the center;
seventy times for Metal in the west;
and fifty times for Water in the north.
From ninety [repetitions] down to fifty in the northern direction,
these together constitute one complete cycle.
If one is not yet satiated, one should recite further as described above.
Recite no more than two times;
one will certainly be satiated. In all recitations, begin on a day starting with the trigram *Ren* (壬), taking the hour of *Yin* (寅) as the first.
The person of ultimate attainment establishes the fixed divisions, which may be arranged according to the four seasons.
Recite the method as described above.
Furthermore, when first wishing to recite it:
One should cause the tongue to move by biting it, thereby severing the silence;
when reciting, if there is saliva,
one should swallow it down.
It is not to be considered strange that one urinates only once every two, three, or four days as described in later sutras;
for now, all sentient beings alike receive the yin and yang energies to form their bodies.
Now that one has received the vital breath from the Celestial Kitchen,
it is for this reason that the entire body is able to perform beneficial tasks.
When first reciting, by the third day, one’s strength gradually becomes weakest.
After this day, one will immediately obtain [visions] for seven days;
having already come and gone, they will certainly be accomplished without doubt.
For a hundred days thereafter, one will dream of obtaining the finest flavors and foods in the world.
After one hundred days, one will dream of obtaining celestial food and drink;
the nose will constantly perceive the fragrance of heavenly cuisine.
Upon the completion of three hundred days, one's merit will be perfected.
One will immediately attain the fruit of the Way.
I only pray that you will exert yourself to sever the three poisons and cultivate compassion for all sentient beings.
Take refuge in and pay homage to the Triple Gem.
Constantly keep Amitābha Buddha in mind;
after one year, you will surely behold the Buddha.
This is certain and beyond doubt.
The Tripiṭaka Master spoke thus:
"If one wishes to seek unsurpassed bodhi..."
For one who is single-mindedly focused in meditative concentration,
the only obstacle is consuming too much food, which hinders the cultivation of dhyāna and prevents the attainment of the fruits of the Path.
First, according to the *Sūtra on the Divination of Contemplation*,
after having repented of one's transgressions, one must go to a mountain forest, a quiet valley, a secluded room, or a still chamber; there,
one first assumes the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka*).
Place the left hand upon the right hand,
close both eyes,
and bring the upper and lower teeth together so they touch.
Sitting upright in a balanced posture,
one first relies upon the four periods of the morning, evening, midnight, and noon;
according to the cardinal directions, one collects the mind and silently recites as if beneath a ritual altar.
One must not allow the mind to grasp at external objects.
[The recitation] ranges from ninety times down to fifty times;
if one is not yet satiated, it should not exceed two rounds until one is satisfied.
While reciting correctly, from time to time during the intervals, use the tongue to sever the external flow of saliva and swallow it.
To remain free from hunger and thirst, constantly recite one verse at a time during the periods of the outer hours—specifically at the *you*, *zi*, and *wu* watches.
Having eaten these three kinds of food for seven full days, one will immediately know whether the dharma has been accomplished:
whether it was due to a lack of sincerity or because one possesses merit.
For those who are without fault;
for those who have attained meditative concentration;
for those who have reached the fruit of the Path.
If one recites this verse three hundred and sixty times, one will not suffer from hunger.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke this incantation:
Nataḥ nataśa svāhā | ūnaṭi mahāūnaṭi svāhā. Regarding the aforementioned dharmas for receiving and maintaining [the precepts], one must wear clean and pure clothing.
Within a quiet chamber,
burn various kinds of named incense to make offerings to all the worthy sages and saints;
thereafter, recite the aforementioned dharma twenty-one times.
To complete one life-span, one must be extremely reverent;
for seven days, one must not speak with others.
One must be very cautious regarding this.
One must not see women, animals, or the like.
It is as if one who is parched with thirst were to obtain cow’s milk, dates, and gruel to drink.
If one wishes to know the name of the kitchen deity, [one should proceed as follows].
I shall now speak it:
Namo daśagāthakamāya svāhā. Namo mārgamañjūṣāya. Namo jīva-pratisthita-prabhātābhimukha-śunye.
The earth resounds and the celestial drums roll;
for two weeks, they partake of the jade nectar.
Those good sons and good daughters who wish to practice this method of the three storehouses [should do so].
First, observe the fast and precepts with a sincere mind.
Then, with utmost sincerity, burn priceless incense and silently recite the name of the aforementioned kitchen deity.
He performed prostrations and repentance, seeking protection and assistance;
he performed forty-nine prostrations in the kitchen.
Having thus completed this, he clearly distinguished their forms and names.
Thereafter, one should recite the verse.
If one simply recites the verse for one hundred days,
one will not suffer from hunger for those one hundred days.
If one seeks the causes and conditions for transcending the world and swiftly realizing the four fruits of the path,
one must receive and uphold the names of the kitchen deities.
Ordinary people do not realize that by means of the mouth, they can utter the names of these deities.
The mind then becomes disrespectful;
if the mind treats the supreme Dharma with contempt,
that Dharma will not be perfected and shall never come to an end.
On the fourth wu and fourth ji, the intestines are firm and blocked; on the fourth ren and fourth gui, do not eat.
On the sixth jia and sixth ding, the great stomach is full. On the fifth geng and fifth xin, the five viscera are pure;
the celestial immortals and jade maidens serve my spirit. The celestial officials provide a traveling kitchen to nourish my body.
May my countenance always be full and joyful, and may I increase in years and longevity for tens of thousands of years.
This is the *Buddhabhāṣita-bhakta-triparivarta-dhāraṇī-mantra*.
*Namo hradate tara ye / dhu lu dhu lu mahā dhu lu / oṃ kṣipra-haṇi-śve / oṃ kṣipra-haṇi-śve.* This dhāraṇī is contained within the separate practice manual (*pṛthag-caryā-vidhi*).
Having gone to a secluded place where no one is present,
at the time of dawn, he washes his bowl with pure water and brushes the inside of the bowl with a willow branch.
Take a handful of pure grass and spread a clean cloth over it;
then place the bowl face down upon it.
Facing east, sit in the full lotus posture.
Close your eyes and place your tongue against the upper palate.
Silently recite the aforementioned mantra one hundred and eight times.
Upon opening his eyes and looking,
the food was immediately there; he ate it to his heart's content,
and if there were any leftovers, [he set them aside].
Recite the preceding mantra seven times.
Then, with eyes closed, contemplate in your mind:
"The remaining food shall go back to its original place. As soon as this is done, it departs.

*The Sūtra on the Three Storehouses Spoken by the Buddha*, one fascicle. Regarding the assistance for the three storehouses (*trikoṣṭhaka*), it was the family tradition of the Gu clan. Subsequently, the Dharma was separately transmitted to a certain Brahmin, who obtained the essential principles for assisting the three storehouses.
Avalokiteśvara accepts my Dharma; the Rishi bestows my provisions.

Following the colors of the five directions—blue, black, red, white, and yellow—one obtains them by blending [the ingredients] into a pill. One should protect oneself from all defilements by reciting this mantra: [Mantra follows]

Namo Buddhāya, Namo Dharmāya, Namo Saṃghāya, Namo Śrīśāya, Svāhā. Recite this fifty times; it is as if one sees the Tathatā (Suchness) and yet does not see it as suchness. Existence is not empty; existence is neither self-existent nor existent through another. Svāhā. If one fears that evil Māras may come to afflict people and create obstacles, one should recite this mantra fifty times.
